html:
Porcelain made at Jingdezhen in Jiangxi, south China, the town that became the world's greatest porcelain centre. It took its name in 1004 from the Jingde reign of a Song emperor, when its kilns already supplied the court.

The town had the two things porcelain needs: fine white clay from nearby hills, including kaolin, and pine forests to fire the kilns. Under the Song it made pale blue-green wares. Under the Yuan potters began to paint with cobalt imported from Persia, creating blue and white ware. The Ming set up imperial kilns here, which made porcelain for the palace in vast amounts.

Private kilns made far more for export. Jingdezhen ware went by sea to Southeast Asia, India, the Middle East and East Africa, and from the 1500s to Europe in Portuguese ships and then in those of the Dutch East India Company. European potters tried for centuries to copy it, and in English the word "china" came to mean porcelain.
